name: Tilted Universes and the Whimper
description: Homogeneous universes whose matter drifts through the surfaces of homogeneity, so that an observer riding with it sees a lopsided sky. In the simplest of them, Farnsworth's dust of 1967, those surfaces turn from spacelike to timelike across a Cauchy horizon, and the light rays along the horizon end where the density and the curvature are finite: a whimper, as George Ellis and A. R. King named it in 1974.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The world ends, in the last line of T. S. Eliot's poem "The Hollow Men", "Not with a bang but a whimper" [eliot1925]. George Ellis and A. R. King asked the same of its beginning, in a paper of December 1973 titled "Was the big bang a whimper?" [ellis1974]. A homogeneous universe has a family of surfaces on which every point is like every other, and in the best studied of them the matter sits still in those surfaces, as the galaxies do in Friedmann's universes [king1973]. King and Ellis had laid out in November 1972 the universes whose matter drifts through the surfaces, which they called tilted, and the question in the title grew out of them [king1973, ellis1974].¶What does an observer riding with tilted matter see? Such a universe "may appear to be inhomogeneous to a fundamental observer", King and Ellis wrote, whose counts of radio sources or galaxies "will look inhomogeneous", "even though the space-time and its contents are spatially homogeneous in a strict mathematical sense" [king1973]. The tilt is a boost: the velocity of the matter makes a hyperbolic angle $\beta$ with the normal to the surfaces, and the matter crosses them at the speed $c\tanh\beta$ [king1973, ellis1974]. The simplest tilted universes are of Bianchi's type V, the open Friedmann universe with one direction picked out, and David L. Farnsworth had found the one filled with dust in 1967 [king1973, collins1974, farnsworth1967]. In his coordinates the surfaces of homogeneity are those of constant $u = ct + Cr$, the dust moves along the lines of constant $r$, and $\tanh\beta = C/X$ for a scale factor $X(u)$ [anton2023].¶Followed back in time, the tilt of Farnsworth's universe grows until the dust crosses the surfaces of homogeneity at the speed of light, at $X = C$, and there the surfaces themselves turn null [ellis1974]. By 1969 L. C. Shepley had seen that the universe is singular there although the density of the dust stays finite [shepley1969, ellis1974]. Earlier still the surfaces are timelike, so the symmetry that made the universe the same at every place now makes it the same at every time, and the null surface between the two regions is a Cauchy horizon [ellis1974, collins1974]. Ellis and King proved that tilted universes of every Bianchi type of class B, type V among them, can have such a horizon, showed that a light ray along it comes to an end after a finite affine distance, with the density finite and the curvature finite in the frame of the matter, and named that end a "whimper" [ellis1974].¶Their picture of a whimper is painted on the flat plane of special relativity [ellis1974]. Paint one world line that misses a point $p$, then boost it about $p$ by every rapidity, so that the plane fills with matter that is the same along each hyperbola at a fixed interval from $p$ [ellis1974]. Those hyperbolas are the surfaces of homogeneity, spacelike above $p$ and timelike beside it, and the two null lines through $p$ divide them [ellis1974]. The world lines cross one null line, the horizon, and crowd toward the other, so that a light ray running down the horizon toward $p$ "crosses an infinite number of matter world lines in a finite affine distance" [ellis1974]. With the painted line taken straight and the two missing dimensions put back, the picture is Farnsworth's solution with no dust in it, $X = u$ and $Y = u + C$, which is flat [farnsworth1967, anton2023].¶So was the big bang a whimper? Ellis and King counted the freedom in the starting data and found "an open set of models" with one in each of those Bianchi types, a proportion they called "not negligible" [ellis1974]. C. B. Collins, at Oxford, worked through the type V universes with pressure in January 1974 under the title "Tilting at cosmological singularities", and charged the cosmologists who had dismissed Shepley's example with "wishful thinking and dangerous extrapolation" [collins1974]. Ellis and King had also seen the weak point: a photon sent down the horizon arrives with infinite blueshift, so a small disturbance should turn the whimper into a "little bang" that most of the matter misses [ellis1974]. S. T. C. Siklos redid the count with the horizon itself as the starting surface and settled it in 1978: the universes with a horizon "depend on two fewer parameters than the most general solution", so that whimpers are "not stable features" of homogeneous universes [siklos1978].¶The 1.36 million quasars that Nathan Secrest and five colleagues took from the catalogue of the WISE satellite in 2021 are lopsided across the sky in the direction of the dipole of the microwave background, with an amplitude "over twice as large as expected" from our own motion [secrest2021]. Chethan Krishnan, Ranjini Mondol, and M. M. Sheikh-Jabbari answered with "dipole cosmology", a universe with a cosmic flow built into it, "an axially isotropic, tilted Bianchi V/VII$_h$ cosmology" in the setting of King and Ellis [krishnan2023, allahyari2025]. Run backward, such a universe reaches either a big bang of diverging curvature or, in the words of A. Allahyari and three colleagues, "a much milder singularity, the whimper singularity", depending on the sign of its shear [allahyari2025].

related.text: The homogeneous universes these belong to. Bianchi's types sort the surfaces of homogeneity, and the tilt is the freedom of the matter to drift through them, which type I forbids [king1973].
Farnsworth's dust with no tilt. At $C = 0$ it is Friedmann's open universe of dust, with $\eta$ its conformal time [anton2023].
The flat model with no tilt. At $C = 0$ its lines of matter all pass through one event, and it is Milne's universe.
The flat model is a part of Minkowski space, filled with straight world lines that all pass one event at the same distance [ellis1974].
A vacuum with the same anatomy. Taub's homogeneous universe lies between two stationary regions, across null surfaces of homogeneity [collins1974, siklos1978].
Kasner's universe is of Bianchi's type I, which has no tilted universes [king1973].
The horn is the same slicing of hyperbolic space by horospheres, with $y$ and $z$ made periodic and no tilt.

coordinates.name: Homogeneous Time

parameters.description: Tilt, a length: the matter crosses the surfaces of homogeneity with the speed $cC/X$ along $r$, and with $C = 0$ it is at rest in them
Scale factor along $r$, a length; the surfaces of homogeneity are spacelike where $X^2 > C^2$, null where $X^2 = C^2$, and timelike where $X^2 < C^2$
Scale factor of the planes of $y$ and $z$, a length ($Y > 0$)

coordinates.convention: We use Farnsworth's comoving coordinates $(r, y, z)$, each a number, with the time $u = ct + Cr$, a length, where $t$ is the proper time of the matter, which moves along the lines of constant $r$, $y$, and $z$. The surfaces of constant $u$ are the surfaces of homogeneity, and the scale factors $X(u)$ and $Y(u)$ are left free. A prime is a derivative along $u$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Farnsworth's Dust

parameters.description: Tilt, a length ($C > 0$): the dust crosses the surfaces of homogeneity with the speed $cC/X$ along $r$, and with $C = 0$ the universe is Friedmann's open universe of dust
A length that sets the amount of dust ($W > 0$): the mass density $\rho$ has $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 3/\left(W\,X\sinh^4(\eta/2)\right)$
Scale factor along $r$, a length, $X = Y - C\,dY/du$ for $Y = W\sinh^2(\eta/2)$; the surfaces of homogeneity are timelike where $X < C$ and spacelike where $X > C$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, r, y, z)$, each a number, with $\eta$ the parameter of Friedmann's open universe: the planes of $y$ and $z$ have the scale factor $Y = W\sinh^2(\eta/2)$, and $u = ct + Cr = \tfrac{1}{2}W\left(\sinh\eta - \eta\right)$ for the proper time $t$ of the dust, so that $du = Y\,d\eta$. The surfaces of constant $\eta$ are the surfaces of homogeneity, and the dust moves along the lines of constant $r$, $y$, and $z$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Flat Model

parameters.description: Tilt, a length ($C > 0$): every line of the matter is a straight line of Minkowski space that passes one event, the origin of the inertial coordinates, at the distance $C$

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(u, r, y, z)$ of the homogeneous chart with $X = u$ and $Y = u + C$, Farnsworth's solution with no dust, $W = 0$. The lines of constant $r$, $y$, and $z$ are straight lines of Minkowski space, with $u/c$ the proper time along each. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -\left(du - C\,dr\right)^2 + u^2dr^2 + e^{-2r}\left(u + C\right)^2\left(dy^2 + dz^2\right)

coordinates.name: Inertial

parameters.description: Tilt, a length ($C > 0$): every line of the matter is a straight line that passes the origin at the distance $C$, and they are all tangent to the hyperboloid $x^2 + \xi^2 + \zeta^2 - c^2T^2 = C^2$

coordinates.convention: We use inertial coordinates $(T, x, \xi, \zeta)$ of the flat model, with $T$ a time and the others lengths: $cT + x = (u + C)e^{-r}$, $cT - x = (u - C)e^{r} + (u + C)e^{-r}\left(y^2 + z^2\right)$, $\xi = (u + C)e^{-r}y$, and $\zeta = (u + C)e^{-r}z$ for the coordinates $(u, r, y, z)$ of the flat model. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cT$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{T}$ means $d(cT)/d\lambda$.
